changeLog.reason: MISSING SAFETY TAG: hypoglycemic. The testosterone cypionate label (Depo-Testosterone, Pfizer) carries an explicit Drug Interactions entry: 'Changes in insulin sensitivity or glycemic control may occur in patients treated with androgens. In diabetic patients, the metabolic effects of androgens may decrease blood glucose and, therefore, insulin requirements.' The vocabulary defines hypoglycemic as 'can cause or potentiate hypoglycaemia' — potentiation of insulin/sulfonylureas is squarely in scope, and this is a genuine drug-drug rule (a user logging testosterone alongside insulin or a sulfonylurea should get a glucose-monitoring caution). The effect is amplified, not attenuated, at the 300-500mg/week the app documents, since androgen-driven improvement in insulin sensitivity scales with dose. The prior agent's risk-tag survey covered hepatic, cardiovascular, haematological, endocrine and CNS domains but never considered the glycaemic domain at all, and the same gap is replicated verbatim on the enanthate record. Separately, for the notes (no vocabulary tag fits, flag for v2): the same label section documents that androgens lower thyroxine-binding globulin, producing falsely low total T4 with normal free T4. That is not immunoassay interference so assay-interfering does not strictly apply, but the app lists a monitoring panel and a user could be started on levothyroxine on the basis of a distorted total T4. Everything else on this record is sound — the dht-derived, hepatotoxic, qt-prolonging (androgens shorten QTc) and nephrotoxic rejections all hold, dea=3 and aa=[100,100] are correct, and store=reframe is right: the FDA's 28 Feb 2025 class-wide labeling change confirms both the bp-raising tag and that this is an approved drug with a mainstream indication, so exclude would be wrong.

MISSING SAFETY TAG: hypoglycemic — identical to the cypionate record and for identical reasons. Androgen potentiation of insulin and oral antidiabetic agents is class labeling that applies to testosterone enanthate exactly as it does to cypionate; the ester is cleaved by serum esterases before the hormone reaches the receptor, so no pharmacological distinction exists. The prior agent's own stated principle — that these two records must stay tag-identical or interaction rules will fire inconsistently depending on which ester the user logged — is correct and is precisely why this omission must be fixed on both records together rather than on one. Everything else on this record is sound; dea=3, aa=[100,100] and store=reframe are all correct. Minor notes-level inaccuracy with no tag consequence: the notes state enanthate has a ~7 day half-life, but the record's own halfLifeHours field says 108 (4.5 days), which is the more commonly cited figure for testosterone enanthate; the 7-vs-8-day framing overstates how close the two esters are, though it does not change any tag.

STORE MIS-SCOPED: ok should be reframe. The vocabulary defines ok as 'ships in a store build as written' and says FDA-approved drugs are fine when 'used for their approved indication'. Only one of this entry's three dose rows is an approved indication. Prometrium/Utrogestan are approved for secondary amenorrhoea and for endometrial protection in postmenopausal women on estrogen; 'Sleep Optimization: 100-200mg' and 'Men (adjunct): 10-20mg' are not, and the summary states the indication as 'BHRT, sleep optimization, and as a DHT modulator in men'. The 'Sleep Optimization' row is the same optimization-framing pattern the prior agent correctly said must be stripped from the testosterone records, and the pros list carries an efficacy claim ('Reduces DHT conversion in men (modest)') that the human data do not support — I checked, and while progesterone is a competitive 5a-reductase inhibitor in vitro (24-62% inhibition of DHT synthesis in human fibroblasts), the in-vivo effect on serum 5a-reduced androgens in humans is minimal. This is a scoping and claims issue, not a safety one: progesterone is an approved, non-scheduled substance, so neither the Play unapproved-substance rule nor Apple 1.4.3 is triggered, and exclude would be clearly wrong. But reframe is the correct bucket, since reframe exists precisely for entries needing the indication restated as the approved one. The tag set itself is correct and I am not changing it: hpta-suppressive is well applied and is in fact the key safety fact behind the men's row (progesterone is anti-gonadotropic, so an app in the TRT space recommending it to men is recommending something that suppresses the axis it is trying to support); neuropsychiatric, cyp3a4-substrate and absorption-sensitive are all solid; 5ar-inhibitor is weak but correctly applied under the asymmetry rule with the uncertainty on record; and withholding teratogenic is right, since micronized progesterone is given deliberately in pregnancy for luteal support. dea=null and aa=null are correct.

Missing hypoglycemic. The agent's important negative on hematocrit-raising is correct and verified (hemoglobin, hematocrit and reticulocytes unchanged in trials), but it stopped at the EPO-lineage question and missed a documented human glycaemic signal at the exact dose this app records. Brines et al., Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled trial in type 2 diabetes: 4 mg/day subcutaneous for 28 days -- matching the entry's 'Neuropathy and Pain: 4mg' row -- produced a significant HbA1c improvement (p=0.002) alongside improved cholesterol/HDL ratio and triglycerides. The mechanism work in Goto-Kakizaki rats found HbA1c reduced ~20% with increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from isolated islets, i.e. an insulin-secretion mechanism rather than a sensitivity shift alone. The users of ARA-290 are diabetic and small-fibre neuropathy patients, who are overwhelmingly already on insulin, a sulfonylurea or a GLP-1, so the additive-hypoglycaemia rule is exactly the warning that should fire and currently does not. This is also internally inconsistent with the same batch: hypoglycemic was applied to Humanin on rodent/primate evidence with no human dosing data, while withheld from ARA-290 where a human RCT at the documented dose exists -- under the vocabulary's stated uncertainty-asymmetry rule ARA-290 is the stronger of the two. I deliberately do NOT recommend insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue: the secretion mechanism rests on rodent islet data, and that structural tag would group an 11-amino-acid innate-repair-receptor agonist with insulin and sulfonylureas and likely drive dose-adjustment rules that are not warranted. hypoglycemic alone carries the safety meaning. Secondary, outside the tag schema: the monitoring row ('Pain scales, nerve conduction studies, CRP, CBC') should gain fasting glucose and HbA1c. Tags otherwise correct; store reframe, dea null and aa null all stand.

Deliberate, self-documented omission that defeats the record's own tagging strategy. The agent tagged pct1 by union of constituents (SERM tags from tamoxifen + clomiphene) but then knowingly withheld the hCG tags, even though dose row 3 reads 'TRT discontinuation: HCG 500IU 3x/wk x 3 wks then Nolva + Clomid standard'. Its stated reason (avoid attributing hCG properties to the two SERM-only variants) is exactly the false-positive-vs-false-negative trade the vocabulary resolves in the opposite direction ('When genuinely uncertain, apply the tag... A false negative produces a missing one'). If the rules engine reads protocol-level tags — which the agent itself concedes is the fallback path — a user on the TRT-discontinuation variant gets NO estradiol/aromatization warning, NO HPTA-suppression warning (hCG suppresses endogenous LH/FSH by negative feedback while the user believes they are restarting), NO haematocrit warning, and critically NO assay-interference warning: administered hCG makes serum and urine hCG assays read positive and confounds germ-cell/trophoblastic tumour-marker interpretation for days after the last dose. That last one is the single highest-value missing warning in the batch because it produces a spurious pregnancy or cancer-marker result with no obvious cause. Adding the five hCG tags costs at most a redundant caution on the two Test-only variants; withholding them silences four real ones. store=exclude, dea=null and aa=null are all correct and unchanged.

Missing renal tag. The Mounjaro and Zepbound labels carry a Warnings and Precautions section for Acute Kidney Injury: postmarketing reports of AKI and worsening chronic renal failure, in some cases requiring haemodialysis, the majority in patients whose GI adverse reactions (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) caused volume depletion, with an explicit instruction to monitor renal function during dose initiation and escalation. Nothing in the current tag set fires any renal warning, and the record's own monitoring line (HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipids, weight) omits creatinine/eGFR entirely. This is the tag that should drive the highest-yield co-administration rule for this compound — tirzepatide plus an NSAID, ACE inhibitor/ARB, or diuretic during a vomiting episode is the classic triple-whammy AKI setup, and dose escalation is when it happens. `gastric-emptying-delaying` and `hypoglycemic` do not cover it. Everything else on tirz is sound: the refusal to use `thyroid-hormone` for the C-cell boxed warning is correct (wrong tag), the reading of `absorption-sensitive` as own-absorption-only is correct for a SC peptide (the outbound oral-contraceptive interaction is genuinely carried by `gastric-emptying-delaying`), and store=ok is right for an approved drug documented at label doses.

Over-cautious exclude on an approved prescription drug, and internally inconsistent with the same agent's own calls elsewhere in the batch. hCG is FDA-approved (chorionic gonadotropin for injection; Pregnyl, Novarel) with approved indications in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, prepubertal cryptorchidism, and ovulation induction. Vocabulary section D states the default plainly: 'Approved prescription drugs -> ok or reframe', and defines reframe as being for 'compounds with a legitimate supervised medical use whose current entry is written for performance use' — which describes this record exactly. The Google Play rule the agent leans on prohibits hCG promoted IN CONJUNCTION WITH anabolic steroids or weight loss; reframe is the mechanism that removes precisely that conjunction (delete the 'Pre-PCT primer: 500IU 3x/week' and 'Blast restart: 1000-1500IU 3x/week' rows, drop the on-cycle/pre-PCT framing and the 'Maintains fertility potential during cycle' pro, and state the approved indications). The agent's justification — 'a genuinely reframed hCG entry would be a different record' — is equally true of tamoxifen and clomiphene, whose entries are 100% PCT-framed and which it nonetheless scoped as reframe with instructions to strip the cycle scheduling. Applying a stricter standard to hCG removes a genuinely important male-fertility and hypogonadism reference from a harm-reduction app. All five tags (peptide, aromatizing, hpta-suppressive, hematocrit-raising, assay-interfering) are correct and unchanged, as are dea=null and aa=null.

MISSING INTERACTION TAG: warfarin-potentiating. Androgen class labelling carries this explicitly — Depo-Testosterone (testosterone cypionate, an INJECTABLE, NON-alkylated AAS), oxandrolone and Anadrol all state 'Androgens may increase sensitivity to oral anticoagulants. Dosage of the anticoagulant may require reduction.' The oxandrolone multidose study in 15 warfarin-treated subjects found S-warfarin half-life 26h -> 48h and AUC 4.55 -> 12.08 ng*hr/mL, with microscopic haematuria in 9/15 and gingival bleeding in 1/15; onset within 2-3 days of starting OR stopping. Critically, the mechanism is NOT 17alpha-alkylation-dependent, so the tagger's (correct) reasoning that drostanolone is a non-alkylated oil ester does not exempt it. At the documented 300-500mg/week, a user on warfarin or presenting for anticoagulation review gets no bleeding-risk warning at all without this tag. Everything else in this row verifies clean: dea=3 correct (all AAS are Schedule III), aa [62,25] is the conventionally cited rodent figure, store=exclude correct, and withholding 17aa-oral, hepatotoxic and aromatizing is right for a non-alkylated non-aromatising injectable. aromatase-inhibitor is thinly evidenced in vivo but I am NOT recommending removal — it is the conservative direction for an AI-co-administration/E2-crash rule.

TWO OMISSIONS. (1) warfarin-potentiating — same androgen-class oral-anticoagulant labelling as drostanolone (verified on the injectable testosterone cypionate label, so it is not alkylation-dependent); methenolone is an AAS and at 400-600mg/week injectable this is a live bleeding-risk interaction with no warning currently attached. (2) neuropsychiatric — mood, aggression, sleep and anxiety disturbance is a supraphysiologic-AAS class effect, and the SAME batch applied this tag to drostanolone. There is no pharmacological basis for treating methenolone at 400-600mg/wk differently, so the omission is an internal inconsistency that silently drops the CNS warning for this compound only. VERIFIED CORRECT, no change needed: methenolone acetate is 1-methyl (1-methyl-5alpha-androst-1-ene) with a 17-BETA acetate ester and is NOT 17alpha-alkylated (confirmed) — withholding 17aa-oral is right; dea=3 correct; aa [88,44] is the conventionally cited figure; store=exclude correct; the entry's 'FDA-approved for immune deficiency conditions' claim is indeed unsupportable and should be struck. I am deliberately NOT recommending removal of hepatotoxic even though the pharmacology argues against it (published sources state oral primobolan does not carry the hepatotoxic burden of alkylated orals, because the 1-methyl route trades bioavailability for hepatic safety) — stripping a caution the entry's own monitoring row already implies is the wrong direction of error in a harm-reduction app. Keep it, but grade it as the lowest severity band if the engine supports grading.

TWO OMISSIONS. (1) neuropsychiatric — the published LGD-4033 clinical literature lists psychiatric symptoms as a recognised adverse-effect category alongside hepatotoxicity, cardiovascular and endocrine effects, with reports of hallucinations and psychotic-like behaviour and commonly reported sleep disturbance. Independently, LGD is the most suppressive common SARM and the app documents 15-20mg/day (15-20x the 1mg dose that already suppresses), so hypogonadal mood disturbance during and after use is expected. RAD-140 received this tag in the same batch on weaker evidence than exists here, so the omission is also an internal inconsistency. (2) cardiotoxic — the same SARM adverse-effect literature documents cardiovascular complications including myocardial infarction, and LGD produces the most pronounced HDL suppression of the SARMs in this batch. The vocabulary's uncertainty-favours-tagging rule applies squarely. Verified correct and unchanged: dea=null (the SARMs Control Act has been introduced repeatedly since 2018 and has still not passed — SARMs remain federally unscheduled), aa=null, hepatotoxic (8 of 15 published SARM DILI cases are LGD; a 2024 Cureus case of pruritic jaundice after 3 months of high-dose use), hpta-suppressive, lipid-suppressing, virilizing, teratogenic, store=exclude. The duplicated/conflicting dose rows the tagger flagged are real and present in the source record.

MISSING cardiotoxic, and unlike most class-based cardiac tags this one is CONFIRMED by compound-specific published human cases, not extrapolated: acute myocarditis in a 16-year-old who presented to the ED with chest pain after his FIRST dose of RAD-140 (Cureus, 2022), and myopericarditis following RAD-140 use (JACC: Case Reports, 2024). That is direct cardiac risk beyond blood pressure — exactly the tag's definition — and it is the most severe rapid-onset harm documented for any compound in this batch, occurring after minimal exposure rather than requiring chronic supraphysiologic use. Its absence means a RAD-140 user with chest pain or dyspnoea gets no cardiac flag from the rules engine while the same batch tags drostanolone cardiotoxic on purely class grounds. Verified correct and unchanged: dea=null (SARMs are not federally scheduled), aa=null is the RIGHT call — the '90:1' in the entry summary is a tissue-selectivity ratio and encoding it on the Hershberger testosterone=100:100 scale would propagate a category error into any comparison table; hepatotoxic is confirmed (6 published RAD-140 DILI cases including biopsy-proven canalicular cholestasis); neuropsychiatric correctly applied; store=exclude correct.

MISSING INTERACTION-MECHANISM TAG: cyp3a4-inducer. This is a labelled interaction on every somatropin product (Norditropin, Genotropin, Omnitrope, Serostim): GH increases CYP450-mediated clearance (antipyrine data), and 'the clearance of compounds such as sex steroids, corticosteroids, anticonvulsants and cyclosporine may be especially increased, resulting in lower plasma levels of these compounds'; hGH-receptor-agonist labelling identifies CYP450 3A4 and/or 1A2 as the isoenzymes where the effect is most significant. The downstream harms are all under-treatment, which is why a missing tag here is dangerous rather than merely incomplete: loss of seizure control on an anticonvulsant, transplant rejection or graft loss on cyclosporine, hormonal-contraceptive failure, and inadequate glucocorticoid cover (GH separately enhances hydrocortisone-to-cortisone conversion and inhibits 11beta-HSD-1, so replacement doses may need increasing). Of every compound in this batch, somatropin is by far the most likely to be co-administered with genuine prescription therapy — it is the only FDA-approved drug in the set — so this is the highest-value missing interaction tag in the batch. Verified correct and unchanged: store=reframe is right and an exclude here would be over-scoped (somatropin has real approved indications: adult GHD, HIV wasting, short bowel, Turner); dea=null is correct federally, with the tagger's 21 USC 333(e) and state-level notes worth keeping; withholding hypoglycemic is CORRECT — GH raises glucose and drives insulin resistance, so applying it would invert the warning, and the absent hyperglycemic/glucose-raising tag is a genuine v1 vocabulary gap rather than a tagging error.

TWO OMISSIONS, one of them the most consequential miss in the batch.

(1) MISSING 'assay-interfering'. Exemestane and its metabolites cross-react in sex-steroid immunoassays. Mandic et al. (Ann Clin Biochem 2017, 'Falsely elevated serum oestradiol due to exemestane therapy') found falsely elevated oestradiol in most E2 immunoassays, with one platform giving false elevations in ~20% of patients on therapy; a 2025 study (PMC12187492 / PMID 40114653) found markedly falsely elevated androstenedione in ALL FOUR immunoassays tested at the standard 25mg dose, with the magnitude correlating to serum exemestane concentration. This is literal immunoassay cross-reactivity — precisely what the tag definition describes ('interferes with lab immunoassays, e.g. biotin') — not a borderline call. The safety consequence is direct and closed-loop: this entry's monitoring row is 'E2 sensitive assay, Total T, Free T', and the entry's whole purpose is titrating an AI against an E2 number. A user on exemestane reads a falsely HIGH E2, concludes the AI is underdosed, escalates from 12.5mg E3D toward 25mg EOD, and crashes their true E2 — producing exactly the joint pain, lipid deterioration, mood collapse and bone loss the entry lists as cons. Without the tag no rule tells anyone the number is unreliable or that LC-MS/MS is required. Note the internal inconsistency: the same batch applied 'assay-interfering' to dutasteride on the weaker analyte-shift rationale (PSA halving is a true biological effect, not assay artefact) while missing it here where the mechanism is textbook cross-reactivity.

(2) MISSING 'absorption-sensitive'. The Aromasin label directs 25mg once daily AFTER A MEAL because a high-fat breakfast raises exemestane AUC by 59% and Cmax by 39% versus fasted. That is a ~60% exposure swing driven purely by administration timing, on a compound this entry documents at 12.5-25mg being titrated to an E2 target — the same over-suppression failure mode as above. Meets the tag definition ('its own absorption is meaningfully altered by co-administered drugs/minerals/food') more strongly than several compounds in this batch that did receive it.

CONFIRMED CORRECT, no change: 'lipid-suppressing' is right and the entry's 'more favorable cholesterol profile' pro is wrong in absolute terms — meta-analysis of RCTs gives HDL-C WMD -6.03 mg/dL (95% CI -7.77 to -4.29, p<0.001) and the manufacturer's own clinical pharmacology reports HDL down 6-9%. Withholding 'aas' is correct (exemestane is a 6-methylene androstadienedione and its 17-hydro metabolite is an AR agonist, but it is not scheduled, not classified as an anabolic steroid, and tagging it would misfire the Schedule III default and the AAS store filter); 'virilizing' is the right vehicle for the androgenic signal. cyp3a4-substrate, teratogenic, neuropsychiatric, dea=null and store='reframe' all confirmed.

ONE MISSING TAG AND A WRONG STORE CALL, both flowing from the same fact — this entry documents a protocol that deliberately drives the user hyperthyroid.

(1) MISSING 'bp-raising'. The omission is internally inconsistent with the batch's own reasoning. 'cardiotoxic' and 'neuropsychiatric' were applied to NDT on the over-replacement scenario, and the entry's monitoring row states outright: 'TSH typically suppresses — guide dose by Free T3 target'. That instruction, followed literally, targets a suppressed-TSH state on a product that contains real T3 (~9mcg T3 per grain; 1-2 grains documented) — i.e. iatrogenic subclinical thyrotoxicosis. The tachycardia, widened pulse pressure and systolic rise of thyroid excess follow from exactly the same premise as the arrhythmia risk that WAS tagged; you cannot accept the premise for one and reject it for the other. The T3 record correctly received 'bp-raising' on this reasoning. Aggravating factor: NDT's monitoring row tracks heart rate but NOT blood pressure, unlike the T3 record which tracks both — so with no tag and no monitoring line, nothing in the app prompts a BP check on the one thyroid product whose stated dosing target is TSH suppression. (I accept the batch's distinction for the T4 record, which stays clean: its documented 25-150mcg range is ordinary replacement and its entry does not instruct dosing to suppression. NDT's entry does.)

(2) STORE 'ok' -> 'reframe'. The regulatory premise behind the 'ok' call is out of date and the batch's own note flagged it as the thing that could flip the decision. On 6 August 2025 the FDA formally determined that animal-derived thyroid products — naming Armour Thyroid, NP Thyroid and Nature-Throid, all three listed in this record's 'aka' — have no approved biologics license application and therefore cannot legally be marketed, and directed the ~1.5 million users to transition to an approved product. A follow-up FDA letter of 11 March 2026 removed the hard removal deadline in favour of risk-based enforcement while manufacturers pursue a BLA, with draft guidance promised; DTE therefore remains prescribable and dispensable today (Sept 2026) but is now, unambiguously and by explicit federal determination, an FDA-UNAPPROVED drug. Google Play prohibits apps that promote unapproved substances 'irrespective of any claims of legality' — continued legal availability under enforcement discretion is exactly the claim of legality that rule declines to accept. And this entry is written promotionally, not neutrally: its pros include 'Some patients report superior symptom relief vs T4 alone', 'Often preferred by functional medicine practitioners', and 'Standardized by USP for iodine content' — that last one actively misrepresents the regulatory status by implying a standards-based approval the product does not have (USP potency conformance is not FDA approval, and batch potency variability is the well-known objection to DTE). Reframe required: state the unapproved/BLA status explicitly, delete the promotional pros, and replace 'TSH typically suppresses — guide dose by Free T3 target' with guideline dosing, since that instruction is the mechanism by which the entry produces the AF and bone-loss risk it does not warn about. Also worth correcting in text: the ~4:1 T4:T3 ratio is far more T3-weighted than the human thyroid's own ~14:1 output, which is the actual pharmacological objection to NDT and appears nowhere in the entry. Remaining tags, dea=null and aa=null are correct.

STORE 'reframe' -> 'exclude'. The batch flagged this as its closest call and invited a second opinion; on the verified facts it fails the vocabulary's own reframe test on both prongs.

The vocabulary permits 'reframe' for a peptide with no approval anywhere ONLY where there is 'a large legitimate clinical-research literature and no performance framing'. P021 (Ac-DGGL-Amide adamantane, a CNTF/peptide-6 derivative from Khalid Iqbal's lab at the NYS Institute for Basic Research) has NEVER entered human trials — no published Phase I/II/III, no human pharmacokinetics, no human dose-response, no human safety data, with the literature concentrated in the originating research program and sparse independent replication. A single-lab preclinical rodent literature is not 'a large legitimate clinical-research literature'; it is the opposite of the case the reframe path was written for. And the framing is not neutral reference: the entry supplies an explicit human dosing protocol ('Research dose: 100-200mcg') for a compound with zero human exposure data, then adds stack language ('Some researchers combine it with Dihexa for a comprehensive neuroplasticity approach') and cognitive-enhancement positioning aimed at healthy users.

The risk is not hypothetical bureaucratic risk. The entry's own con list contains 'Theoretical cancer risk from uncontrolled neurogenesis' — the single most important warning on the record — and v1 has no proliferative/oncogenic tag to carry it, so nothing fires. Shipping a numeric human dose for a never-in-human compound whose stated principal hazard cannot be tagged is precisely what Google Play's prohibition on promoting unapproved substances 'irrespective of any claims of legality' and Apple 1.4.3's prohibition on encouraging consumption are aimed at. Reframing cannot fix it, because after removing the dose row, the stack language and the enhancement framing there is no supervised clinical indication left to restate — unlike exemestane, cabergoline or T3, which have real approved indications to fall back to. That is the structural difference between 'reframe' and 'exclude' here.

Tags ('peptide', 'neuropsychiatric'), dea=null and aa=null are all correct and need no change; the neuropsychiatric call on target-organ grounds is sound, and correctly withholding 'gh-axis' is right. A v2 'proliferative/oncogenic-risk' tag should be raised for this record.

FALSE POSITIVE, contradicted by direct human data rather than merely unproven. The batch applied 'aromatizing' on the uncertainty asymmetry plus the entry's own text, and explicitly recorded it as a soft call — but the asymmetry rule covers genuine uncertainty, and here there is positive human evidence of absence at doses far above anything this app documents.

In the Marx et al. proof-of-concept trial, oral pregnenolone escalated to 500mg/day for four weeks (2.5x to 50x this entry's 10-200mg/day rows) produced ~4x serum pregnenolone, ~3x pregnenolone sulfate, ~5x allopregnanolone, >4x progesterone and ~16% DHEAS — with NO increase in oestradiol, testosterone, free testosterone, DHEA, androstenedione or cortisol. Downstream conversion past progesterone is enzyme- and tissue-limited and does not occur systemically at supplement doses. The tag was therefore applied on the strength of the entry's speculative claim 'Can convert to any steroid — unpredictable conversion pathway', which is the thing that is factually wrong and should be corrected in the entry text rather than propagated into a structured tag that an interaction rule will consume. Left in place it can push a user toward unnecessary aromatase-inhibitor co-use — a real, if second-order, harm on a harm-reduction app, and 'a tag is a property of the compound, not an opinion about it'.

Removing it also resolves the inconsistency the batch acknowledged (tagging aromatizing but not virilizing): on the evidence neither applies, so the record is now consistent. Do NOT add 'virilizing' — the same trial rules out androgen conversion at 500mg/day. Note the same evidence also disposes of the entry's 'Can increase cortisol' con (cortisol was unchanged).

KEEP 'neuropsychiatric' — it is the genuinely well-supported tag here, and the >4x progesterone and ~5x allopregnanolone rises are the real pharmacology: GABA-A positive allosteric modulation by allopregnanolone versus GABA-A negative / NMDA positive modulation by pregnenolone sulfate, which explains the entry's contradictory 'anxiolytic' and 'may worsen anxiety' cons and the additive sedation risk with alcohol and benzodiazepines. Store 'ok', dea=null and aa=null are correct. Separately, the duplicated pros/cons arrays and the conflicting dose rows ('Neurological Support: 10-30mg/day' beside 'Cognitive / Mood: 50-100mg/day' for the same indication) need cleaning regardless of tagging.

MISSING LIPID TAG — highest-value omission in the batch. The record concludes resveratrol/pterostilbene is metabolically inert and applies only interaction tags. But this is a combined record and the entry documents pterostilbene at 50-150mg/day, explicitly calling it 'preferred'. Riche et al. 2014 (Evid Based Complement Alternat Med, NCT01267227), 80 subjects, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled, 6-8 weeks: pterostilbene monotherapy RAISED LDL-C by 17.1 mg/dL (P=0.001) and the paper states this was independent of dose — i.e. the effect was present in the 50mg-twice-daily (100mg/day) arm, squarely inside the range this entry documents. The rise was attenuated in subjects already on a lipid-lowering drug and was abolished when pterostilbene was co-administered with grape extract (P=0.47). The v1 definition of lipid-suppressing is 'meaningfully suppresses HDL and/or raises LDL', so a +17 mg/dL LDL rise in a human RCT qualifies directly and is not a marginal asymmetry-rule call. VIP is the principal inhibitory NANC neurotransmitter of the gut and is the transmitter responsible for neurally induced gastric relaxation; VIP-receptor-mediated fundic relaxation is demonstrated with competitive VIP antagonists, and VIP-induced gastric relaxation is ~90% blocked by indomethacin, confirming a defined prostaglandin-dependent pathway. The opposing consideration the record raised — secretory diarrhoea and accelerated transit — is a small-bowel/colonic secretory phenomenon and does not cancel proximal gastric accommodation, so the two effects are not actually symmetric. Concrete consequence of leaving it off: no additive-delay or additive-GI-burden caution fires when VIP is combined with a GLP-1 agonist, and GLP-1 co-use is highly likely in this app's population. unexpressibleRules.missingTag: sympathomimetic (present in vocab, applied to ZERO of 131 compounds) — plus a `tachycardic`/`hr-raising` tag and a `catecholamine-sensitizing` tag
unexpressibleRules.note: This rule cannot fire on any axis. (1) There is no clenbuterol record — I grepped all 11 batches for clenbut/ephedr/yohimb/albuterol/DNP: zero hits. The catalogue contains no stimulant of any kind, so `sympathomimetic` is a dead tag with no members. (2) T3 is deliberately NOT tagged `qt-prolonging` (correctly — thyrotoxicosis SHORTENS QTc) and NOT `electrolyte-disturbing` (thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis judged too rare). So neither participant carries either tag. The t3 note itself concedes the real mechanism is untaggable: 'the additive-adrenergic risk with clenbuterol/stimulants is real and should be captured in the interaction text instead.' Interaction text is not consumable by a rules engine. Note the qt-prolonging holders are nolv, berberine, insulin, dasatinib, oxytocin — a set that has nothing to do with this rule.

unexpressibleRules.missingTag: sympathomimetic (zero members) — the compound records themselves are missing, not the tag
unexpressibleRules.note: Same root cause. The AAS side is fully tagged (`aas` + `cardiotoxic` + `bp-raising` on ~20 records) but there is no counterparty in the dataset. A rule written as `aas AND sympathomimetic` returns the empty set forever. This is a corpus gap, not a vocabulary gap: clenbuterol, ephedrine, yohimbine, DNP, albuterol, caffeine and ADHD stimulants are all absent, and they are the compounds this population actually stacks with AAS.

`absorption-sensitive` is defined in the vocabulary as 'ITS OWN absorption is meaningfully altered' — strictly inbound. There is no outbound tag, so `gastric-emptying-delaying` marks the perpetrator but nothing connects it to a victim. Three separate notes independently hit this wall (larazotide: 'v2 would benefit from an alters-absorption-of-others tag'; tirz: 'the outbound absorption interaction has no tag'; retatrutide: 'confirm the rule engine reads it that way'). Worse, the named victims — oral contraceptives, oral naltrexone (pt141's label interaction), levothyroxine — either aren't in the catalogue or are only tagged on the inbound side. A workaround rule `gastric-emptying-delaying AND absorption-sensitive` misfires: it would pair semaglutide with resveratrol/fisetin/ala, whose absorption is altered by fat and minerals, not by gastric emptying.

unexpressibleRules.missingTag: delays-absorption-of-others / chelating-agent, plus mineral records (calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc) and a PPI record
unexpressibleRules.note: t4 correctly carries `absorption-sensitive`, but every interferer its own cons name — 'Absorption affected by food, coffee, calcium, iron' — is absent from the 131 records. The one in-catalogue perpetrator is ala, whose cons say 'Should be separated from thyroid medication by 4 hours', and ala is tagged only `absorption-sensitive` (inbound, describing ALA's own food dependence). The ala note explicitly records the inversion: 'the direction of the levothyroxine interaction in the cons is the reverse... v1 has no tag for impairs absorption of other drugs'. So the single expressible instance of this rule inside the catalogue is unexpressible.

unexpressibleRules.missingTag: the biotin/B-vitamin record itself; plus splitting `assay-interfering` into immunoassay-crossreacting vs analyte-shifting, plus an affected-analyte field
unexpressibleRules.note: There is no biotin record — zero hits across all batches — so the canonical instance of the rule the tag was named for cannot fire. Separately, `assay-interfering` is overloaded across three incompatible mechanisms and a single rule consuming it will emit wrong advice: true cross-reactivity (npp, boldenone, proviron, trenace/trenenan, estriol → 'repeat on LC-MS/MS' is right); genuine analyte shift (dutast halves PSA, creatine raises real creatinine → LC-MS/MS is useless, the correct action is 'reinterpret/double the value'); and administered-analyte (hcg2 causes true-positive pregnancy tests). Both the dutast and creatine notes flag this and ask for the split. There is also no field naming WHICH lab is affected, so no rule can tell the user what to re-check.

unexpressibleRules.rule: AI + oral AAS compounded HDL suppression
unexpressibleRules.missingTag: an `oral` route tag; plus a potency split on `aromatase-inhibitor` (therapeutic-AI vs weak-intrinsic-AI)
unexpressibleRules.note: Two independent failures. (1) 'Oral' is not expressible in the tag layer at all. `17aa-oral` is the only proxy and it deliberately excludes the orals that matter here: primooral and primo (1-methyl), proviron (1α-methyl), yk11 (methoxyethylidene, not 17-alkyl), and every oral SARM (osta/lgd/rad140/andarine). Route lives in the source `medium` field, which is null on 12 records and is not part of the tagging. (2) `aromatase-inhibitor` conflates real AIs (ai1, exemest) with steroids carrying weak intrinsic anti-aromatase activity (mast, mastenan, proviron). Since those three are ALSO `aas` and `lipid-suppressing`, the rule self-fires on a single logged compound, and the genuinely important warning the mast/proviron notes describe — that stacking Masteron or Proviron on top of anastrozole crashes E2 — is indistinguishable from the HDL rule.

unexpressibleRules.missingTag: none — the tag is correct and applied to every AAS; the warfarin record is missing
unexpressibleRules.note: `warfarin-potentiating` is applied consistently across all 20+ androgens and to nolv, t3, t4, ndt, berberine, resveratrol, fisetin, quercetin, dasatinib, melatonin-ther, nalt. But there is no warfarin, DOAC, aspirin or any anticoagulant record in the catalogue, so the rule has nothing to pair against and can only fire against a free-text external med list that this dataset does not model. The identical dead-end applies to `nitrate-contraindicated` (applied to mt2, pt141, nalt, akg2 — with no nitrate and no PDE5-inhibitor record anywhere) and to `insulin-secretagogue-or-analogue` on the sulfonylurea side. Every section-C tag except the CYP3A4 trio is designed to pair with a drug class the catalogue does not contain.

unexpressibleRules.missingTag: a severity/magnitude qualifier on `hepatotoxic` (and the `oral` route tag above)
unexpressibleRules.note: Expressible but wrong-scoped in both directions. Scoped to `17aa-oral` it matches only 5 compounds (oxan, stanozolol, dianabol, anadrol, turinabol) and misses the oral SARM stack that is the best-documented DILI cluster in this very dataset — the lgd note cites '8 of the 15 published SARM DILI case reports are LGD-4033, including a case requiring transplant evaluation'. Scoped to `hepatotoxic` it matches ~19 compounds and will fire equally on acarbose + LDN-era naltrexone as on anadrol + stanozolol, because the tag is a flat boolean. The notes repeatedly presuppose a grading that does not exist: primo — 'an order of magnitude below any true 17aa oral — if the rules engine grades severity, this should be the lowest band'; primooral — 'downstream rules should treat this as a much lower hepatic tier'; trenace/trenenan — hepatotoxic applied at 'moderate confidence'. None of that survives serialization to a string array.

The detection half works: `19-nor` on nandro, npp, trenace, trenenan, yk11, and `prolactin-raising` on those plus hexarelin, ghrp2, ghrp6, mk677. What cannot be expressed is the resolution half. Cabergoline and bromocriptine — the entire reason those two records exist in this catalogue — are tagged `dopamine-agonist`, which also has to serve as an impulse-control/fibrosis flag, and the caberbromo note states the problem directly: 'there is no prolactin-lowering tag and prolactin-raising would be inverted and dangerous, so this entry carries no prolactin tag at all despite prolactin being its entire purpose'. The npp record's own cons say 'Cabergoline may be needed' and nothing in the tag layer connects the two records. Also note yk11 carries `19-nor` but not `prolactin-raising`, so a rule keyed on the risk tag rather than the structural tag silently drops it.

The stacking rule fires correctly. What is unexpressible is the offset, which is the clinically interesting case in this catalogue: the telmisartan note states 'ARBs LOWER haematocrit (they are used for post-transplant erythrocytosis), which is precisely why the entry pairs it with TRT; do not let any rule infer the opposite', and the rapamycin note states 'rapamycin will LOWER haematocrit, the opposite direction from most of this app's catalogue'. Neither is representable, so an engine sees TRT + telmisartan as an untouched polycythaemia risk and cannot explain the pairing. bonomarlot compounds this — it is tagged `hematocrit-raising` on an entry whose own text claims a bidirectional effect ('both too high and too low').

missingForTools: DATA-INTEGRITY: 6 records whose `store` FIELD contradicts the store call written in their own `notes`. A build filter reads the field, so these ship wrong. hcg2 field='reframe' / notes='store=exclude, and this is the clearest call in the batch' — this is the dangerous direction: it ships the one entry Google Play prohibits by name (hCG in conjunction with anabolic steroids). Also progesterone field='reframe'/notes='store=ok'; p21pep field='exclude'/notes="STORE: 'reframe' rather than 'exclude'"; ndt field='reframe'/notes="STORE 'ok' on platform grounds"; pt141 field='reframe'/notes='STORE ok... Caveat recorded rather than escalated to reframe'; estriol field='reframe'/notes='Store = ok... it needs no rewrite'.

DATA-INTEGRITY: 5 records whose `tags` array contradicts their own notes. pregnenolone — notes say "'aromatizing' applied on the uncertainty asymmetry" but tags contain only ['neuropsychiatric']; the tag is missing. In the other direction, tags were applied that the notes say were rejected: vip has `gastric-emptying-delaying` while notes say 'I did not tag gastric-emptying-delaying'; dianabol has `electrolyte-disturbing` while notes say 'Considered electrolyte-disturbing... and left it off'; dasatinib has `electrolyte-disturbing` while notes say 'Considered and not applied: electrolyte-disturbing'; taurine and akg2 both carry `hypoglycemic` while both notes say the effect 'was judged below the threshold for hypoglycemic'. Any merge that produced these needs a notes-vs-tags assertion in CI.

DEDUPE KEY — blocks every 'total load' computation a PCT builder needs. Six records are the same molecule (tc, te, tprop, testsusp, sustanon, testpellets) and they carry THREE different tag sets: tc/te have 13 tags including `cyp3a4-substrate` and `hypoglycemic`; tprop/testsusp/sustanon have 11 and lack both; testpellets has 14 and uniquely adds `electrolyte-disturbing`. Identical hormone, different warnings depending on which ester the user logged — the exact failure the te note tried to prevent between cypionate and enanthate. Same problem: aod9604 ≡ hghfrag (the aod9604 note flags it); nandro's `aka` covers NPP while npp is a separate record; primo and primooral are both methenolone; trenace/trenenan. There is no `molecule_id`/`same_as` field, so androgen load, 17aa hepatic load and 'am I already on a 19-nor' are all uncomputable.

PROTOCOL/COMPOSITE MODEL — pct1 is not a compound (medium=null, halfLifeHours=null, doses are multi-drug taper strings) but is stored in the same shape and tagged with the union of tamoxifen + clomiphene properties. There is no `is_protocol` flag and no `constituents` array, so an engine treats it as a substance and double-counts against separately logged nolv/clom/hcg2. The note itself hedges: 'if the rules engine resolves protocols by expanding constituents rather than by reading protocol-level tags, that is the better mechanism and these tags should be treated as a fallback' — the dataset provides neither the flag nor the constituent list to choose between them. Its third dose row's hCG properties were deliberately omitted from the tags, so the union is knowingly incomplete.

HPTA DIRECTION — the single most damaging omission for a PCT builder. `hpta-suppressive` is applied to the recovery TOOLS as well as the suppressants: hcg2, gonadorelin, kissp and kisspeptin54 all carry it, identically to trenbolone. A builder keyed on that tag excludes its own instruments. There is no `hpta-stimulating` tag and no directionality qualifier; four separate notes flag it (kissp: 'the correct warning is do not dose continuously, not the AAS-style expect suppression, plan a restart... the tag alone is misleading and the note carries the meaning'; kisspeptin54: 'bidirectional HPG agents cannot currently be distinguished from true suppressants'). The actual PCT drugs (nolv, clom, enclo) carry only `serm`, which also matches raloxifene, which is not a PCT drug.

SUPPRESSION MAGNITUDE + RECOVERY TIME — no field exists. trenace ('near-total'), nandro ('profound and slow-recovering'), osta ('minimal suppression' contradicted by its own cons) and oxan all reduce to the same boolean. A PCT builder cannot choose SERM vs SERM+hCG, set duration, or rank compounds without it.

HALF-LIFE UNUSABLE FOR PCT TIMING — halfLifeHours is null or absent on 59 of 131 records, including pct1, testpellets, insulin, estriol and every Khavinson peptide; `medium` is null on 12 including testpellets and insulin. Where present it is wrong for the record's own scope: nandro carries 180h (decanoate) on a record whose aka includes NPP; stanozolol carries 9h on a record whose dose row is '25-50mg/day oral or 50mg EOD injectable'. PCT start date is a function of ester clearance and cannot be computed.

DOSES ARE UNPARSED FREE TEXT — no numeric amount, unit, frequency, duration or route fields. pct1's rows are literally 'Nolvadex 40/40/20/20/20/20mg + Clomid 50/50/25/25mg'. A protocol builder cannot read a taper out of that, and a store filter cannot mechanically delete 'the performance row'.

DOSE-ROW → TAG PROVENANCE — the vocabulary's own rule of application makes tags conditional on documented doses ('the app documents 300-500mg/week performance dosing, so it qualifies'), but nothing records WHICH dose row justified which tag. The consequence is circular and unhandled: a compliant store build deletes the performance rows, and the tags those rows justified (tc `cardiotoxic`, sustanon `hematocrit-raising`, oxan `bp-raising`, primo's whole risk set) silently become unsupported. The reframed entry and the tag set cannot both be correct.

NO SEVERITY OR CONFIDENCE FIELD ON TAGS — the notes are saturated with grading language that a flat string array discards: 'my softest tag', 'lowest-confidence', 'precautionary', 'deliberate false positive', 'if the rules engine grades severity, this should be the lowest band'. An engine cannot distinguish isotretinoin's boxed-warning `teratogenic` from enclo's ('practically relevant only if used in women, which is not the documented use'), or oxan's `warfarin-potentiating` (documented ~85% warfarin dose reduction) from boldenone's (pure class inference). This is the structural omission that most degrades every rule listed above.

STORE FILTER CANNOT ACT — `store` gates but does not describe. For all ~60 'reframe' records the required edits exist only as prose in `notes`, with no structured field naming the dose rows to delete or the sentences to remove (cerebrolysin's 'Requires sourcing from countries where it's approved', chonluten's post-COVID claim, thymalpha's 'Active illness / Cancer adjuvant: 1.6mg' row, testpellets' revenue line, nalt's 'especially valuable on oral AAS', argireline's single 'SubQ (experimental): 50-100mcg' row). There is also no `reframed`/review-state boolean, so a build cannot tell an un-rewritten entry from a rewritten one, and no escalation flag for the entries the notes explicitly refer up (pda, ghrp6, p21pep, ndt, sustanon).

NO JURISDICTION DIMENSION — `store` and `dea` are single scalars for a global build. Several 'ok' calls are US-only by the notes' own admission and are wrong elsewhere: dhea ('prescription-only in several countries (UK, Canada, Australia) — so ok is a US-market call'), melatonin-ther, nad/NMN, akg2/NAC. sustanon is marked 'reframe' with the note conceding 'Sustanon specifically is NOT FDA-approved in the US — if the store build is US-targeted... this should drop to exclude'. rhgh's dea=null is federal-only while the note flags 21 USC 333(e) and state-level scheduling of hGH.

NO approval_status FIELD — `store` is derived from approval status but the status itself is never stored, so it cannot be re-derived, audited, or updated when it changes. It has already changed under this dataset: ss31's entry still reads 'Clinical trials ongoing — not FDA approved' after elamipretide's Sept 2025 approval; aod9604, thymalpha and dac all moved on and off FDA's Category 2 503A bulks list; retatrutide and cagrilintide are pending decisions. Needed values: approved / withdrawn-commercial / withdrawn-safety / unapproved / investigational / grandfathered-pre-1938 / compounding-restricted.

NO prescription_only FLAG DISTINCT FROM `dea` — the notes draw this line repeatedly ('prescription-only is a different thing from scheduled, so dea is null') but nothing encodes it. To a filter reading `dea: null`, dasatinib, isotretinoin, raloxifene, rapamycin, telmisartan, t4 and semaglutide are indistinguishable from spermidine and creatine.

NO wada_prohibited FLAG — asserted in ~20 notes (bpc S0, tb5/tbnouveau S2, mk677 S2, osta/lgd/rad140, card, hcg2, dac, keto-dhea S1, dhea, igf1lr3) and explicitly requested twice ('there is no wada-prohibited tag, and I'd argue for one'). Any athlete-facing or 'will this test positive' feature has no data to run on.

NO REMS / PREGNANCY-PROGRAM FLAG — isotretinoin's iPLEDGE (dual contraception, monthly pregnancy testing) and dutasteride's crushed-tablet handling prohibition and 6-month blood-donation deferral are the highest-consequence handling requirements in the corpus and have no home outside prose.

NO CARCINOGENIC / PROLIFERATIVE-RISK TAG — requested independently in 9 notes (card, igf1lr3, tb5, tbnouveau, bpc, bpc157sys, dihexa, p21pep, follistatin, epi, spermidine). For card it is the defining fact of the compound ('GSK abandoned development specifically due to carcinogenicity') and the record still ships a dose row; `hepatotoxic` was applied as an acknowledged partial proxy that will be misread as coverage.

NO HYPERGLYCEMIC / INSULIN-RESISTANCE TAG — requested in 8 notes across the entire GH-secretagogue class (cjc, ipa, ghrp2, ghrp6, serm2, tesam, mk677, rhgh, dac) plus rapamycin. `hypoglycemic` is the only glucose tag and points the wrong way, so a diabetic-user rule built from these tags silently misses every GH agent — despite those records' own monitoring lines all asking for fasting glucose.

NO IMMUNOSTIMULANT TAG — requested in 5 notes (ll37, thymalin, vilon, crystagen, thymalpha, selank). `immunosuppressive` is the only immune tag and applying it would invert the meaning, so the autoimmune-disease and transplant-recipient caution — which the crystagen note calls out as surviving 'only in prose, which no rules engine can consume' — has no representation at all.

NO thrombogenic TAG — requested in the nolv note ('venous thromboembolism (a boxed warning)... arguably tamoxifen's single most important acute risk') and forced raloxifene's `cardiotoxic` to be applied off-definition as a stand-in ('strictly read the tag does not fit'). Also applies to clom, enclo, estriol and the oestrogen class.

NO bp-lowering / hypotensive TAG — flagged in 5 notes (caberg, caberbromo, telmisartan, taurine, vip). taurine's own monitoring says 'Blood pressure (taurine lowers it — monitor if on antihypertensives)' and telmisartan is in the same catalogue; the additive-hypotension rule between two in-catalogue compounds cannot be written.

NO cortisol-raising / HPA-AXIS TAG — flagged in 5 notes (hexarelin, ghrp2, ghrp6, dsip, pregnenolone). ghrp6's cons say 'Most cortisol and prolactin elevation of common GHRPs' and its monitoring row asks for cortisol; only the prolactin half is taggable.

MISCELLANEOUS SCHEMA DEFECTS: (a) 12 records (dianabol, anadrol, turinabol, mastenan, primooral, testsusp, sustanon, slupp332, raloxifene, isotretinoin, caberbromo) carry an `aa_note: null` key that the other 119 do not — schema drift from a partial merge. (b) The akg2 id belongs to GlyNAC but reads as alpha-ketoglutarate, colliding conceptually with the separate akglutarate record; the note flags it as 'a copy-paste id collision' that will break any id-keyed rule. (c) `cls` is unreliable as a role proxy: card is filed under 'SARMs' though it is a PPARδ agonist with no AR activity, and hcg2 sits in 'Ancillaries — AIs and SERMs' though it is neither. (d) The Khavinson series carries at least three wrong peptide sequences (cardiogen listed as KEDW not AEDR; sigumir listed as AEDG, which is Epithalon's sequence, so two records claim the same molecule; chonluten listed as Ventfort's KED).
